topic.name: Properties of Line Integrals of Vector-Valued Functions

question.text:
The path $C_1$ consists of a the line segment from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(1,2),$ and the path $C_2$ consists of a line segment from the point $B(1,2)$ to the point $D(1,3).$

Given that $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \dfrac{7}{2},$ evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf{F}(x, y) = (2x-3y) \,\mathbf{i} + (x+y)\,\mathbf{j},$ and $C = C_1\cup C_2.$
question.explanation:
We will use the fact that \[ \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}. \]

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path $C_1$ is the line segment from $A$ to $B.$ It can be parametrized as \begin{align*} \mathbf{r}_1(t) &= \mathbf{a} + t \big( \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a} \big) \\[3pt] &= \langle 0, 1 \rangle + t \big( \langle 1, 2 \rangle - \langle 0, 1 \rangle \big) \\[3pt] %&= \langle 0, 1 \rangle + t \langle 1, 1 \rangle \\[3pt] &= \langle t, 1+t \rangle \\[3pt] &= t\,\mathbf{i}+(1+t)\,\mathbf{j}, \end{align*} where $0 \lt t \lt 1.$ Along this segment, we have $x = t$ and $y = 1+t.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}_1(t)) &= (2x-3y) \,\mathbf{i} + (x+y)\,\mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= (2t-3(1+t))\,\mathbf{i} + \left(t+(1+t)\right)\,\mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= (-3-t)\,\mathbf{i} + \left(2t+1\right)\,\mathbf{j}. \end{align*}

Computing the derivative, we get the following: \begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_1(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( t \right) \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( 1+t \right) \mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j} \end{align*}

We can now compute the dot product: \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}_1(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'_1(t) &= \big( (-3-t)\,\mathbf{i} + \left(2t+1\right)\,\mathbf{j} \big) \cdot \big( \mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j} \big) \\[3pt] &= -3-t + 2t+1 \\[3pt] &= t-2 \end{align*}

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

\begin{align*} \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} & = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r_1}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'_1(t) \, \textrm{d}t + \dfrac{7}{2} \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \left(t-2\right) \, \textrm{d}t + \dfrac{7}{2} \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{t^2}{2}-2t \right]_{0}^{1} + \dfrac{7}{2}\\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{1}{2}-2 - 0 \right] + \dfrac{7}{2} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{7}{2} \\[5pt] &= 2 \end{align*}

question.text: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $KMLK,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the clockwise direction?
question.explanation:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed clockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

\[ C =C_1 \cup \{-C_2\} \cup \{-C_3\}, \]

where $-C_2$ and $-C_3$ are the same paths as $C_2$ and $C_3$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} &= \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} + \int\limits_{-C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} + \int\limits_{-C_3} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} \\[5pt] &= \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} - \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} - \int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} . \end{align*}

question.text: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $UVWU,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the clockwise direction?
question.explanation:

\[ C = C_1 \cup \{-C_2\} \cup \{-C_3\}, \]

where $-C_2$ and $-C_3$ are the same paths as $C_2$ and $C_3$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

question.text:
The path $C_1$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(1,-1)$ to the point $B(1,1),$ and the path $C_2$ consists of a line segment from the point $B(1,1)$ to the point $O(0,0).$

Given that $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = 2,$ evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf{F}(x, y) = (2x+y) \,\mathbf{i} + (x-2y)\,\mathbf {j},$ and $C = C_1\cup C_2.$
question.explanation:
We will use the fact that \[ \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}. \]

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path $C_2$ is the line segment from $B$ to $O.$ It can be parametrized as \begin{align*} \mathbf{r}_2(t) &= \mathbf{b} + t \big( \mathbf{0} - \mathbf{b} \big) \\[3pt] &= \langle 1, 1 \rangle + t \big( \langle 0, 0 \rangle - \langle 1, 1 \rangle \big) \\[3pt] %&= \langle 1, 1 \rangle + t \langle -1, -1 \rangle \\[3pt] &= \langle 1-t, 1-t \rangle \\[3pt] &= (1-t)\,\mathbf{i} + (1-t)\,\mathbf{j}, \end{align*} where $0 \lt t \lt 1.$ Along this segment, we have $x = 1-t$ and $y = 1-t.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}_2(t)) &= (2x+y) \,\mathbf{i} + (x-2y)\,\mathbf {j} \\[3pt] &= (2(1-t)+(1-t)) \,\mathbf{i} + ((1-t)-2(1-t))\,\mathbf {j} \\[3pt] &= (3-3t)\,\mathbf{i} + (-1+t)\,\mathbf {j}. \end{align*}

Computing the derivative, we get the following: \begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_2(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( 1-t \right) \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( 1-t \right) \mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= -\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} \end{align*}

We can now compute the dot product: \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}_2(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'_2(t) &= \big( (3-3t)\,\mathbf{i} + (-1+t)\,\mathbf {j} \big) \cdot \big( -\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} \big) \\[3pt] &= -3+3t +1-t \\[3pt] &= -2+2t \end{align*}

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: \begin{align*} \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} & = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} \\[5pt] & = 2 + \int_{0}^{1} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r_2}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'_2(t) \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] & =2+ \int_{0}^{1} (-2+2t) \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] & =2+ (-2t + t^2) \, \bigg|_0^1 \\[5pt] & =2+ \left( 1-2\right) \\[5pt] &=1 \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Line Integral of a Vector-Valued Function Along a Union of Curves

question.text:
The path $C_1$ consists of a the line segment from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $A(1,0),$ and the path $C_2$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(1,0)$ to the point $B(0,-2).$

Given that $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \dfrac{7}{3},$ evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf{F}(x, y) = (x^2+y) \,\mathbf{i} + (x-y^2)\,\mathbf {j},$ and $C = C_1\cup C_2.$
question.explanation:
We will use the fact that

\[ \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}. \]

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path $C_1$ is the horizontal line segment from $O$ to $A.$ It can be parametrized as \begin{align*} \mathbf{r}_1(t) &= \mathbf{0} + t \big( \mathbf{a} - \mathbf{0} \big) \\[3pt] &= \langle 0, 0 \rangle + t \big( \langle 1, 0 \rangle - \langle 0, 0 \rangle \big) \\[3pt] %&= \langle 0, 0 \rangle + t \langle 1, 0 \rangle \\[3pt] &= \langle t, 0 \rangle \\[3pt] &= t\,\mathbf{i}, \end{align*} where $0 \lt t \lt 1.$ Along this segment, we have $x = t$ and $y = 0.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}_1(t)) &= (x^2+y) \,\mathbf{i} + (x-y^2)\,\mathbf {j} \\[3pt] &= (t^2+0)\,\mathbf{i} + (t-0^2)\,\mathbf{j} \\[3pt] &= t^2\,\mathbf{i} + t \,\mathbf{j}. \end{align*}

Computing the derivative, we get the following: \begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_1(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( t \right) \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \left( 0 \right) \mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{i} \end{align*}

We can now compute the dot product: \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}_1(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'_1(t) &= \big( t^2\,\mathbf{i} + t \,\mathbf{j} \big) \cdot \big( \mathbf{i} \big) \\[3pt] &= t^2 \end{align*}

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: \begin{align*} \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} &= \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{1} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r_1}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'_1(t) \, \textrm{d}t + \dfrac{7}{3} \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} t^2 \, \textrm{d}t + \dfrac{7}{3}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{3}t^3 \, \bigg|_0^1 + \dfrac{7}{3}\\[5pt] & = \left(\dfrac{1}{3}-0\right) + \dfrac{7}{3}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{7}{3} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{8}{3} \end{align*}
